analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and restores the laws in place before it.
analysis.headline: The House passed full repeal of the Affordable Care Act 244-185 on July 11, 2012, almost entirely along party lines, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act as if it had never passed, restoring the health care law that existed before 2010 [S2, S4]. That means ending the premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, the ban on denying coverage for preexisting conditions, young-adult coverage on parents' plans, the closure of the Medicare drug-coverage gap, and the taxes that paid for these things [S2, S4]. The House passed it, but the Senate never took a vote and the bill expired with the Congress [S6, S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households would gain most directly, because repeal removes the ACA's taxes — the bill's own findings count 21 new or higher taxes [S4] — including those on investment income and high wages. Large employers would be freed from coverage requirements and penalties. Brand-name drug makers, medical device makers, and Medicare Advantage insurers would be relieved of industry fees and payment cuts the law imposed [S2, S4]. People who preferred to buy skimpier, cheaper plans restricted by the ACA's coverage rules would regain that option.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large employers, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeal restores the pre-2010 legal code, removing every ACA provision including its taxes, mandates, and coverage requirements [S2, S4].
The bill repeals the health-related provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 as well, which carried several of the law's industry taxes [S2, S4].
Supporters argued the ACA raised family premiums by about $1,200 in its first year and would cut Medicare by over half a trillion dollars, harming seniors' access to care [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People who gained coverage or protections under the ACA would lose them with no replacement in the bill: people with preexisting conditions who could finally buy insurance, households receiving premium subsidies, adults under 26 on their parents' plans, low-income people in the Medicaid expansion, and seniors whose drug costs the law reduced [S2, S4]. The general public would also lose the ACA's minimum standards for what insurance must cover [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and newly covered households

drawbacks.text: Repeal would end the ACA's coverage expansions — premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and protections for people with preexisting conditions — restoring the pre-2010 insurance market in which those protections did not exist [S2, S4].
Repeal restores the Medicare Part D drug-coverage gap the ACA began closing, and reinstates the Medicare Advantage payment reductions the bill's own findings describe as $206 billion [S4].

The bill is a straight repeal with no substitute: it repeals the ACA and its companion law and simply restores prior law, so anyone relying on the new coverage would lose it and get nothing in return [S2, S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits of repeal flow to higher-income households and to industries that paid ACA fees and absorbed ACA payment cuts, while the costs fall on the millions of people who got coverage, protections, or lower drug costs from the law. The bill's supporters' own findings argue the ACA raised premiums and cut Medicare too deeply [S4]; those are real criticisms of the ACA. But repeal as written offered no fix for either problem — it just removed the law. Anyone who lost coverage or protections under it would have no alternative in this bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 244-185, but the Senate never scheduled a vote; the bill sat on the Senate calendar until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 244-185 on July 11, 2012, with 239 of 240 Republicans voting yes and 185 of 191 Democrats voting no [S6, S8].

Just before passage, Democrats offered a motion to send the bill back with instructions to add a provision making any member who votes for repeal ineligible for the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program; it failed 180-248, with 239 Republicans voting against it [S6, S7].

The Senate received the bill on July 12, 2012, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar on July 16; no vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S6, S1, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because repeal never became law, the ACA's coverage expansions and its taxes both stayed in place. People with preexisting conditions, subsidized households, young adults on parents' plans, and seniors with reduced drug costs kept what they had; high earners and the industries paying ACA fees kept paying them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with preexisting conditions kept coverage

for.name: Eric Cantor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and brought it to the floor under a rule that allowed five hours of debate and closed it to amendments [S1, S6].

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from July 16, 2012 until the Congress ended [S6].

against.name: Robert Andrews
against.role: Ranking Member, House Health subcommittee efforts; offered the motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back with an amendment requiring members who voted for repeal to give up their own federal employee health coverage; the motion failed 180-248 [S6, S7].

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Signed the Affordable Care Act into law and pledged to veto any repeal, making House passage symbolic in practice.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: 239 of 240 Republicans voted yes, 185 of 191 Democrats voted no, with 5 Democrats crossing over to yes and 1 not voting [S8].

industries.note: Repeal removes the ACA's taxes, which the bill's findings count at 21 new or higher taxes including those falling on upper incomes and investment income [S4]. The savings come from unwinding a law funded largely by those taxes, whose benefits went to lower- and middle-income coverage.

Repeal frees insurers from the ACA's coverage requirements and rate rules, but also ends the subsidized individual market and the individual mandate that brought them millions of new customers [S2, S4]. Insurers would trade regulation for a smaller, less protected market.
Repeal removes the annual fee the ACA imposed on brand-name pharmaceuticals and restores the Medicare drug-coverage gap it began closing, raising seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs [S2, S4].

The bill's findings describe the ACA as cutting $206 billion in Medicare Advantage payments; repeal restores the prior payment levels, and seniors would again pay higher premiums for those plans, as the findings themselves note [S4].
Repeal removes the ACA's sales tax on medical devices, which was carried in the companion law this bill also repeals [S2, S4].
Repeal ends employer coverage requirements and penalties, shifting costs back toward workers and the individually insured market [S2, S4].
